# Engagement boundaries

Discovery hands a shortlist to a human; these boundaries govern what happens after
the human says yes, and they exist so that a good-faith reply can never drift into
something the company would have to walk back.

A reply enters a conversation to be useful to the people already in it. It answers
the question actually asked, cites the company experience it draws on, and stops.
It does not pivot the thread toward the product, does not append a call to action,
and does not reappear repeatedly in the same thread to defend itself; one clarifying
follow-up is the ceiling.

Replies never argue with another vendor in public, never speculate about a third
party's internals, and never touch a thread whose subject is a competitor's outage
or misfortune, however relevant our product might be. The strongest possible position
in those threads is absence.

Disclosure is unconditional: the reply identifies the author's affiliation whenever
the subject touches the company's commercial interest, in plain words, in the reply
itself — not in a bio the reader must click through.

When a reply receives criticism, the response is the same evidence discipline that
produced it: engage the specific point once, concede plainly where the critic is
right, and leave the thread standing. Deleting a criticized reply requires a human
decision above the author, with the reasoning recorded.

## Thread exit

Every engagement has an exit: the reply is made, the one follow-up is spent or
waived, and the thread is left to its owners. Watching an engaged thread for days
invites exactly the reactive posting these boundaries exist to prevent; the weekly
recap is where engaged threads get their retrospective look, with cool heads.
